title: Thai consumers retain routine spending resilience while corruption, safety, unemployment and affordability weaken political-economic legitimacy
source_unit: Ipsos Thailand, What Worries Thailand? September 2026, combining What Worries the World and consumer-sentiment findings
geography: Thailand; Thai consumers and public-opinion respondents as defined by the Ipsos release

observations.period: September 2026; national worries and year-on-year movement

denominator.unit: Thai respondents in the Ipsos What Worries the World and consumer-sentiment source frames; public release does not state a single pooled item base

corruption_concern.unit: percent identifying financial and political corruption as one of Thailand's biggest worries

crime_violence_concern.unit: percent identifying crime and violence as one of the country's three biggest concerns

crime_year_change.unit: percentage-point increase in crime-and-violence concern from September 2025

poverty_inequality_concern.unit: percent identifying poverty and social inequality as a major concern

unemployment_concern.unit: percent identifying unemployment as one of the country's biggest worries; up 11 percentage points year-on-year

legitimacy_stack.value: governance integrity, public safety and economic opportunity are converging into one public legitimacy surface

observations.method: Ipsos country analysis combining published What Worries the World concern indicators with consumer-sentiment measures; the public page does not provide one pooled respondent denominator or full questionnaire in the release.
observations.uncertainty: Concern measures are self-reported and item-specific; they do not establish actual corruption, crime, unemployment, inequality, causal drivers, or policy effects.
observations.subgroup: Thai respondents and consumers represented in the Ipsos country release.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rise in concern can reflect greater salience or news attention rather than worsening objective conditions, and top-ranked worries need not determine voting, purchasing or compliance.

observations.period: September 2026; national direction and economic evaluation

denominator.unit: Thai respondents in the Ipsos country release; item-specific bases are source-defined

wrong_direction.unit: percent saying Thailand is heading in the wrong direction

right_direction.unit: percent saying Thailand is heading in the right direction

economy_bad.unit: percent describing the current economy as bad

direction_economy_gap.value: negative national and economic judgments coexist with continued routine-purchase confidence

observations.method: Ipsos published country-level consumer-sentiment indicators and directional comparisons with August 2026.
observations.uncertainty: Direction and economic judgments are aggregate perceptions; they do not measure GDP, household income, public-service performance, or causal attribution.
observations.subgroup: Thai respondents in the public release's national consumer-sentiment frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: People can distinguish macroeconomic judgment from personal purchasing needs, and negative direction ratings need not imply immediate withdrawal from everyday consumption.

denominator.unit: Thai consumers in the Ipsos consumer-sentiment source frame; item-specific base not disclosed on the public release

everyday_purchase_comfort.unit: percent feeling more comfortable making everyday household purchases than six months earlier

major_purchase_comfort.unit: percent feeling more comfortable making major purchases such as a home or car than six months earlier

financial_situation_stronger.unit: percent expecting their personal financial situation to become stronger over the next six months

financial_situation_weaker.unit: percent expecting their personal financial situation to become weaker over the next six months

consumption_legitimacy_split.value: routine consumption remains more resilient than major commitments and national economic confidence

observations.method: Ipsos consumer-sentiment comparisons with six months earlier, as reported in the country analysis.
observations.uncertainty: Comfort and expectations are self-reported; the release does not observe transactions, debt service, household budgets, credit access, or future purchase completion.
observations.subgroup: Thai consumers in the Ipsos country release.
observations.counterinterpretation: Everyday-purchase resilience may reflect necessity, inflation-adjusted nominal spending, temporary confidence, or substitution rather than improved household room.

denominator.unit: Thai government consumer-subsidy policy context described by Ipsos

consumer_subsidy_extension.unit: billion Thai baht value of the consumer subsidy programme extension cited by Ipsos

policy_legitimacy_route.value: household-purchasing-power policy is presented against persistent worries about corruption, safety, unemployment, inequality and living costs

policy_outcome_boundary.value: the release does not evaluate subsidy take-up, incidence, fiscal sustainability, price effects or durable trust

observations.method: Ipsos country analysis citing the September policy extension as contextual evidence alongside public concern and consumer sentiment.
observations.uncertainty: The subsidy figure is policy context, not an evaluation; no beneficiary, spending, price or welfare outcome is observed in the release.
observations.subgroup: Thai households, consumers and government policy context.
observations.counterinterpretation: A consumer subsidy may stabilize routine spending without resolving institutional integrity, labor-market security or perceived direction of the country.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos primary country analysis with September 2026 concern, direction, economic, spending and policy-context indicators.
Ipsos What Worries the World series provides the comparative concern framework referenced by the Thailand analysis.

boundary: This record adds a comparative consumer-legitimacy route: routine purchasing confidence can remain resilient while corruption, crime, unemployment, inequality, economic pessimism and national-direction judgments deteriorate. The Ipsos public release combines concern and consumer-sentiment indicators without publishing one pooled denominator on the country page; it does not measure objective conditions, realized purchasing, subsidy incidence, causal attribution or durable political trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Ipsos Thailand primary country analysis reviewed for concern ranking, year-on-year changes, national direction, economic evaluation, routine and major-purchase comfort, personal-finance expectations, and cited subsidy context.
